title: Industry I: PEST and Risk in the Environment
keyQuestion: How did Khama change the PEST for De Beers?

reading.name: The PEST Framework: Risk in the Environment (white paper v2)

case.name: Botswana: Building the Foundations of a Diamond Economy

slides: S3 slides (117): political risk, confiscation/expropriation/nationalization, corruption and FCPA, Gigawatt Ecuador dilemma, economic systems, GDP, PPP/Big Mac, Culture Map, technology infrastructure, IP, Botswana PEST 1966

framework.name: PEST with three disciplines
framework.summary: PEST works one layer above the industry: forces that act on every competitor at once, that no firm can negotiate with, and that periodically rewrite the rules. The framework's bad reputation comes from execution (a grid of true, irrelevant facts). It earns its place only through three jobs, each with a discipline: detect change (direction), locate bargaining power, and separate what is given from what can be shaped.

components.name: Political
components.what: Governs political risk: regulation, tax, trade, subsidy, ownership rules, competition enforcement, stability, rule of law. Changes discontinuously, by announcement (India liberalization and Honda; US chip export controls and Nvidia; Botswana consolidating mineral rights).

components.name: Economic
components.what: Governs purchasing power, the cost of capital and relative prices. Matters for what the level does to what customers can afford and what the firm pays to finance itself (end of zero rates; Tesco Fresh & Easy launched into 2007-08). Moves cyclically.

components.name: Socio-cultural
components.what: Governs what people want, will tolerate, and who is doing the wanting. Moves slowly, then all at once as cohorts replace each other; the domain most often noticed too late (lab-grown share of US engagement rings 12% in 2019 → 61% in 2025).

components.name: Technological (three infrastructures)
components.what: What is possible, at what cost, by whom — assessed as three separate infrastructures (Morris & Oldroyd): physical (hardware: raw materials, manufacturing, transport, energy), information (software: communications, data storage and processing), human capital (brainware: education, corporate training, government-business-education cooperation). The shape of the profile, not one score, decides which business models are feasible; opportunities sit in the gaps (M-Pesa).

components.name: Discipline 1: Relevance
components.what: A factor earns a place only if a plausible change in it would change the decision in front of you. Name the decision first. Write every factor as a chain: factor → mechanism → decision affected; anything that cannot complete the chain comes off the page.

components.name: Discipline 2: Direction
components.what: A PEST run once is a photograph. Run it at two points in time and analyze the difference: the level tells you what your position is worth, only the delta tells you whether to change it. An arrow on every row beats a number on every row.

components.name: Discipline 3: Bargaining power
components.what: Every macro factor eventually answers: what happens to each party if this deal is not signed? That outside option decides the split of surplus regardless of what either side deserves. Write the grid twice, once for each side of the table.

components.name: Given vs. built (shaped)
components.what: PEST assumes the environment is exogenous. For geology, demographics and weather that's true; for much of the political, social and technological quadrants it's false, and the falsity is where the most durable advantages are built (lobbying, open standards like Tesla's charging connector, Samsung funding education).

components.name: PEST worksheet (Exhibit 2)
components.what: Seven columns: factor (checkable), then/now, direction (for us specifically), mechanism, decision affected, given or shaped, falsifier.

terms.def: Political, Economic, Socio-cultural, Technological: the layer above the industry — forces acting on every competitor at once.

Variants adding Environmental, Legal, Ethical (and others). Mostly redundant; only Environmental has earned its own letter as an independent driver of cost and demand. Spend no time arguing which letter a factor belongs in.
The threat that political decisions or events in a country will negatively affect the profitability of an investment.
The seizure of corporate assets without compensation (Mugabe seizing 5,000+ farms).
The seizure of property with compensation (Venezuela: ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips forced to abandon investments).
Government seizure of an industry, with or without compensation (Chavez nationalized cement in 2008; Morales nationalized Bolivia's three main airports in 2013).
Gradual seizure through new codes, back-tax claims and administration (Mali vs. Barrick, 2024-25).
What happens to a party if the deal is not signed; the better outside option takes the larger share of the surplus.
Raw materials, manufacturing capability/equipment, transportation networks, energy resources.
Communication technologies and data storage/processing (Estonia's X-Road; UPS left-turn routing).
Education, corporate training, government/business/education cooperation; slowest to build and cannot be imported at will.
A trend changes the rate at which value accrues; a discontinuity changes what creates value at all (a chemically identical lab-grown diamond dissolves the mechanism that set price).
The pattern in which resource wealth harms development; Botswana is the counter-example the class discusses.

Illegal for US firms, citizens, their subsidiaries/agents and issuers of US securities to pay foreign officials to obtain or retain business. Anti-bribery (DOJ) and accounting provisions (SEC). Limited exception for facilitation payments for routine government action.
Similar to but tougher than the FCPA: bars private-sector bribes and applies to both parties, not just the briber.
An exchange between two partners that influences the allocation of resources and involves the use or abuse of public power for private benefit.
'When in Rome, do as the Romans do' vs. 'My way or the highway.'

Law of one price applied to currencies: the exchange rate should equalize the price of the same good (Big Mac index). Deviations suggest over/undervaluation; often fails in the short run and for non-traded goods.
GDP: value of production within a country's borders by domestic or foreign factors. GNP: final goods and services produced by domestic factors, at home or abroad. GDP = C + I + G + NX.

claims.claim: A PEST analysis that could have been written before the decision was identified is not analysis; it is background.
Proposition 1: the environment is only worth analyzing against a decision, and the analysis is complete when every factor is connected to that decision by a stated mechanism.
Proposition 2: movement matters more than level, so run the framework comparatively — across time, and in a negotiation, across both sides of the table.

Proposition 3: the environment is less exogenous than the framework implies; factors a firm builds for itself are worth more than factors it adapts to, because rivals can adapt to the same conditions but cannot easily copy an environment built to suit somebody else.
An environment that was built can be dismantled, sometimes by a party that never appears on the industry map (the laboratory that undid the diamond cartel's scarcity).
PEST should be used before industry tools because it establishes the conditions under which they are valid: which structural features are load-bearing and about to move.

Botswana's 85/15 split moved to parity without a single expropriation because the outside options moved; the relationship survived because the party with growing power used it gradually and stayed predictable.

Botswana today: political and economic quadrants inverted in its favor (capital, expertise, reserves, credibility, own sales channel; counterparty loss-making and written down), but social and technological quadrants deteriorated — a stronger claim on a shrinking asset. Only the comparison shows that.

failures.name: The inventory
failures.what: True facts with no consequence, because no decision was named. Antidote: factor → mechanism → decision chain.

failures.name: The snapshot
failures.what: One grid describing today. Antidote: run it twice and put an arrow on every row.

failures.name: False precision
failures.what: Ten-year forecasts of unforecastable variables. Antidote: state directions and rates of change; if a number is unavoidable, state what would falsify it.

failures.name: Reading technology as a single number
failures.what: Antidote: score the three infrastructures separately and look hardest at the gaps (M-Pesa).

failures.name: Scanning where you already look
failures.what: The most dangerous, invisible from inside: Botswana read politics and economics brilliantly and was overtaken by a laboratory. Antidote: assign someone to the quadrant nobody in the room is qualified to assess.

failures.name: Confusing a trend with a discontinuity
failures.what: Antidote: ask whether a technology changes the cost of doing what we do or the reason customers pay us at all.

failures.name: Treating the quadrants as independent
failures.what: The lab-grown shock was technological change destroying manufactured scarcity at the same moment social change destroyed willingness to pay for scarcity; either alone was survivable. Antidote: look for pairs of factors moving in the same direction.

caseFacts.fact: At independence (1966) Botswana had fewer than a dozen university graduates, under 20 km of paved roads, subsistence agriculture and cattle, and depended on foreign aid. (Slides: 12 km of roads, 22 college graduates, GDP per capita $89, third-lowest in the world.)
caseFacts.why: The 1966 PEST grid: weak on every quadrant, which explains the weak outside option. Note the case and slides give slightly different figures.

caseFacts.fact: Khama consolidated fragmented tribal/private mineral rights under the national government before the scale of diamond wealth was known — 'a strategic gamble rather than a response to obvious opportunity.'
caseFacts.why: The central 'shaped, not given' move: it made the state the sole counterparty for every future discovery (a political act that determined tens of billions over 60 years).

caseFacts.fact: Khama's ethic: 'no palaces and no fancy cars'; Botswana honored the De Beers contract through fiscal strain rather than expanding output or renegotiating unilaterally.
caseFacts.why: Credibility was built deliberately; Botswana as a low-risk counterparty 'looks like a fortunate national character, actually was built' (PEST Ex.3).

caseFacts.fact: 1967 diamonds found at Orapa; 1969 Debswana formed with De Beers holding operational control, output and marketing through the cartel (CSO); 1972 Jwaneng discovered.
caseFacts.why: Botswana traded sovereignty over short-term output for price stability and a route to market it could not otherwise reach.
The case's quantitative spine: equity tracked the shift in outside options. The '?' is the renegotiation question.

caseFacts.fact: Lab-grown diamonds are chemically and visually identical, entered at large discounts; younger consumers question natural diamonds on price transparency, ethics and environment. Case chart: natural production ~1.38 → ~1.08 hundred-million carats (2019-2024) while lab-grown rises.
caseFacts.why: Technological + social factors moving together — the discontinuity that weakens the asset Botswana is negotiating over.

caseFacts.fact: The case's closing question: how much to use increased bargaining power for wins now vs. protecting the future relationship; pivot away from diamonds or lean in?
caseFacts.why: This is where PEST's bargaining-power discipline turns into a recommendation.

strongAnalysis: Answer the Key Question with the 'given vs. built' lens: Khama did not just endure the PEST; he rewrote the political quadrant (consolidated mineral rights → single national counterparty), built the credibility that lowered political risk for De Beers (honoring contracts, no elite enrichment), and used the resulting economic quadrant (revenue, reserves, trained administrators) to move the outside options.

Run the grid twice (1969 vs. 1980s vs. 2026) from BOTH sides of the table: in 1969 Botswana's outside option was 'leave the stones in the ground'; De Beers could source elsewhere → 85/15. By the 1980s De Beers depended on Botswana for a large share of supply → 50/50.

For De Beers, Khama turned Botswana from a political risk into a political asset: a stable, predictable jurisdiction with high-quality deposits. That is why the equity moved and the relationship survived.

2026: Botswana's P and E quadrants favor it, S and T quadrants threaten the asset's value. Recommendation logic: press for gains gradually and predictably, but also use bargaining power to fund diversification and downstream capability, because the claim is getting stronger on a shrinking asset.
Use the failure list against Botswana itself: 'scanning where you already look' — a world-class reader of politics and economics overtaken by a laboratory.

counter.argument: Khama didn't change the PEST; geology did. Diamonds at Orapa and Jwaneng made Botswana valuable, and any government would have captured more over time as revenues grew. The 'credibility' story is hindsight.
counter.response: The deposits explain the size of the prize, not its distribution. Rights were consolidated BEFORE the wealth was known, which is why every discovery became a national negotiation instead of a tribal or private windfall; and the resource-curse pattern shows deposits plus weak institutions usually produce expropriation and collapse (Venezuela output −75% under nationalism). The PEST paper lists Botswana's low-risk reputation as built, not found: consolidated rights, rejection of elite enrichment, contracts honored when breaking them would have paid.

courseMap.text: PEST sits above the industry-level tools and comes first: Five Forces describes structure at a moment, PEST tells you which structural features are load-bearing and about to move; a cost curve assumes a technology, PEST asks how long that holds; WTP assumes customer values, PEST asks whether those values belong to a cohort being replaced.

slideExtras.detail: Macro vs. micro × bilateral vs. unilateral. Bilateral-macro: disputes (South Seas islands), trade battles/WTO cases, war (Russia-Ukraine). Bilateral-micro: FCPA, entry mandates, IP and $ flows, trade agreements. Unilateral-macro: fiscal/monetary policy, price caps, inflation, government instability. Unilateral-micro: expropriation, currency movement, local-goods requirements.

Russia 2023-24 confiscation via 'temporary management' (Danone, Carlsberg's Baltika); Mali 2024-25 creeping expropriation of Barrick's Loulo-Gounkoto (~$500M back-tax claim, 3 tonnes of gold seized, settled Nov 2025, Barrick paid $430M); Niger 2024-25 nationalization of Orano's Somaïr uranium mine (ICSID ruled for Orano Sept 2025).

Argentina's YPF expropriation from Repsol; 2023 US $16.1B judgment and 2025 order to hand over 51% stake, both overturned on appeal March 2026. Venezuela: output fell 31% after 1973-76 nationalizations, rose 55% (1990-98) with foreign capital, fell 75% under Chavez-era oil nationalism; ~1M bpd in 2026.
Top resolutions: Goldman Sachs $1,663M (2020), Ericsson $1,267M, MTS $850M, Siemens $800M US ($1.6B+ total) ...

Solar developer with ~$1M sunk and a 22 MW first phase ($40-45M capex) is asked by a minister for a $1M 'gift'. Options: pay/negotiate, go over his head, redirect to CSR/charity, ignore. At stake: the beachhead, US debt financing, FCPA exposure.

Corruption: pay beyond normal for something to be done, payment to gain a service, abuse of office, pooling systems for bribes. Tipping: extra pay for a task already paid for, recipient will still perform without payment.
Kola Real (AJE) built a beverage business in markets incumbents avoided.

Planned (North Korea, Cuba), market (USA, Switzerland), mixed (governments take over troubled firms vital to national interest). Keynes (demand), Hayek (supply), Friedman (money). China reforms: poverty 60% → 10%.

Output = labor + capital + TFP. GDP = C + I + G + NX (US consumption ~68%). Extremes: Somalia C 133% of GDP, Iran I 44%, Timor-Leste G 61%, Macao NX +42%. FY2025 US deficit 5.9% of GDP; interest > $1T/yr.

China: 12.5 yuan / $3.54 = 3.53 yuan per $ implied vs. 6.84 actual → yuan undervalued. UK £4.59 vs. Japan ¥480 → implied ~104.6 ¥/£ vs. ~200 actual. 'Is the pound overvalued or the yen undervalued?' is a trick question — you need a third currency.

Eight scales: communicating (low vs. high context), evaluating (direct vs. indirect negative feedback), persuading (principles-first vs. applications-first), leading (egalitarian vs. hierarchical), deciding (consensual vs. top-down), trusting (task vs. relationship), disagreeing (confrontational vs. avoids), scheduling (linear vs. flexible time).
Tech infrastructure triangle (physical / information / human). Counterfeiting ~$500B or 6% of goods traded; software $1 illegal for every $2 legal; now pharmaceuticals, baby formula, airplane parts.

P: king turned prime minister, tribes rule most of the country, little central control. E: GDP third-lowest ($89 per capita), currency pula, no known resources, subsistence farming. S: tribes have own culture, family. T: 12 km of roads, 22 college graduates. Then: Khama, the resource curse, Debswana, GDP per capita climbing past ~$15,000 by 2016.
